definition: A container of a header and a set of transactions that extends a blockchain.
wrongs: A private key that authorizes spending from a wallet.
A fee paid to move a transaction ahead of others.
A word list used to back up a wallet.
why: Nodes append accepted transactions by packaging them in a block linked to earlier blocks.
example: A new Bitcoin block contains a header plus the transactions that the successful miner included.
scenario: A miner has a header and a group of valid transactions ready to append to a chain. What container are they building?
scenarioWhy: A block packages a header and transactions so they can extend the chain.

definition: A sequence of blocks in which each block includes a hash linking it to the previous block.
wrongs: A single spreadsheet stored on one company server and edited in place.
A list of passwords kept in a browser.
A folder of unrelated files with no hashes between them.
why: The hash link means a change in an earlier block changes the hash every later block must match.
example: Each campus-demo block stores the hash of the block before it, so students can walk the links back to the start.
scenario: Students can follow a hash in each header back to the first block. What structure are they tracing?
scenarioWhy: A blockchain is the hash-linked sequence of blocks they are following.

definition: The cryptographic hash of a block header, which commits to that header's contents and parent link.
wrongs: The plain-language name of the miner who produced the block.
The wallet address printed on a paper receipt.
The fee a user typed into a wallet screen.
why: Hashing the header covers the parent hash, Merkle root, and other header fields in one digest.
example: A block explorer shows the hash of block 800000, computed from that block's header.
scenario: A node must identify a header by a digest of its parent link, Merkle root, and other header fields. What does it compute?
scenarioWhy: The block hash is the digest of the header and therefore of the fields inside it.

definition: The protocol rules nodes use to agree on which blocks and transactions belong in the ledger.
wrongs: A company's private meeting where one manager edits the accounts.
A password that every wallet owner must share.
A font used to display balances in a wallet app.
why: Without a shared rule for choosing the ledger, nodes could keep incompatible histories.
example: Bitcoin nodes apply proof-of-work rules to decide which competing block becomes part of the ledger.
scenario: Many independent nodes must follow the same rule for which new block is accepted. What is that family of rules called?
scenarioWhy: A consensus mechanism is the shared rule set for agreeing on the ledger's contents.

definition: A consensus method that requires computational effort to produce a block hash meeting a difficulty target.
wrongs: A method that selects the next block producer only from coins locked as stake.
A method in which a named committee signs blocks with no public cost.
A wallet backup made of twelve or twenty-four words.
why: The producer must find a header hash below the target, which takes many hash attempts.
example: Bitcoin miners vary a nonce until the block header's hash is below the current target.
scenario: A network accepts a block only after someone expends computation to hit a hash target. Which consensus method is that?
scenarioWrongs: A closed committee with no public cost
scenarioWhy: Proof of work ties block production to the computational effort of meeting a hash target.

definition: A consensus method that selects validators using locked coins rather than computational puzzles.
wrongs: A method that requires miners to expend hash attempts against a difficulty target.
A method that stores all keys on one exchange server.
A file format for saving an unencrypted private key in email.
why: Validators lock stake and can be rewarded or penalized according to the protocol rules.
example: On a proof-of-stake network, a validator with locked coins is chosen to propose the next block.
scenario: A network chooses block proposers from participants who lock coins, not from hash puzzles. Which method is that?
scenarioWrongs: Storage of every key on one exchange
scenarioWhy: Proof of stake uses locked coins to select validators instead of a mining puzzle.

definition: Software or hardware that stores keys and can build, sign, and broadcast transactions.
wrongs: The blockchain itself, which holds everyone's transaction history.
A block explorer website that only displays public data.
A miner that produces proof-of-work blocks.
why: The wallet manages keys and transaction signing; the ledger of balances lives on the blockchain.
example: A phone wallet holds a student's keys and signs a small test-network payment before broadcasting it.
scenario: A student needs an app that keeps keys and signs a payment, not the global ledger itself. What do they use?
scenarioWhy: A wallet stores the keys and creates signed transactions; it is not the shared ledger.

definition: A key that others can use to check signatures and that can be shared without revealing the private key.
wrongs: The secret key that must stay private because it authorizes spending.
A block hash that identifies a header.
A transaction fee offered to a miner.
why: Signatures made with the private key can be checked with the matching public key.
example: A wallet derives an address from a public key and shows that address to classmates who will send test coins.
scenario: Classmates need a value they can use to verify a signature, and seeing it must not expose the spending key. Which key is shared?
scenarioWhy: The public key verifies signatures and is safe to share, unlike the private key.

definition: A secret key that authorizes transactions for its funds and must remain known only to the owner.
wrongs: A public address that anyone may see in a block explorer.
The Merkle root published in a block header.
The network's difficulty target.
why: Anyone who knows the private key can create valid signatures that spend the associated funds.
example: A student keeps a test-wallet private key offline because anyone who copies it can sign transactions for those coins.
scenario: A token transfer should be signable only by the owner. Which secret must the owner protect?
scenarioWhy: The private key is the secret that creates the signature authorizing the transfer.

definition: A program stored on a blockchain whose code runs when transactions call it, under consensus rules.
wrongs: A paper contract signed with ink and stored in a filing cabinet.
A wallet password written on a sticky note.
A miner hardware manual.
why: Every honest node runs the same contract code, so the resulting state is part of the ledger.
example: A class deploys a small contract that records a vote when students send a transaction to its address.
scenario: Students need on-chain code that every node will run when a transaction calls it. What should they deploy?
scenarioWrongs: A paper form in a cabinet
scenarioWhy: A smart contract is ledger code that nodes execute as part of processing the calling transaction.

definition: Trying to use the same coins in two conflicting transactions that one ledger cannot both accept.
wrongs: Paying a miner a higher fee so one honest transaction is included sooner.
Backing up a seed phrase in two sealed envelopes.
Running two full nodes that store the same chain.
why: Consensus must accept only one history, so the same output cannot be spent twice in the final ledger.
example: Two transactions try to spend the same output, and the network's chosen chain keeps only one of them.
scenario: A shop sees two conflicting payments that spend the same output. What can one consistent ledger finally do?
scenarioAnswer: Accept only one of the two histories
scenarioWrongs: Credit the same coins to both recipients as final
Erase the genesis block to allow both
Turn both payments into extra gas
scenarioWhy: A single ledger cannot treat two conflicting spends of the same coins as both final.

definition: A point where two or more competing chains share a history and then diverge.
wrongs: A backup copy of a seed phrase stored offline.
A wallet setting that shows balances in another currency.
A hardware device that signs transactions.
why: Divergence happens when different blocks claim the same parent and nodes have not yet settled on one branch.
example: Two valid blocks are found at the same height, so some nodes briefly follow one branch and some follow the other.
scenario: Two valid blocks claim the same parent, and different nodes temporarily follow different branches. What is that split called?
scenarioWhy: A fork is the divergence of competing chains that share history up to a common parent.

definition: The first block of a chain, which has no parent block.
wrongs: The latest block at the tip of the chain.
A block that was orphaned and left off the main chain.
Any block that pays a transaction fee.
why: Every later block links back through parent hashes to this first block.
example: Bitcoin's genesis block is the starting block that later blocks reference through the chain of parent hashes.
scenario: Students follow parent hashes backward until they reach a block with no parent. Which block is that?
scenarioWhy: The genesis block is the start of the chain and therefore has no parent.

definition: A binary tree of hashes whose leaves are transaction hashes and whose parents hash their children.
wrongs: A list of wallet passwords stored in alphabetical order.
A hardware tree of mining machines in a warehouse.
A diagram of a company's management ranks.
why: Hashing pairs of child hashes up the tree produces one root that commits to every listed transaction.
example: A Bitcoin block builds a Merkle tree over its transactions so the header can store a single root.
scenario: A block must commit to every included transaction through paired hashes that end in one root. Which structure does that?
scenarioWhy: A Merkle tree hashes transactions upward until one root represents the whole set.

definition: The single top hash of a block's Merkle tree, stored in the block header.
wrongs: The private key of the miner who found the block.
The first transaction fee in the block.
The network port used by a wallet.
why: Changing any included transaction changes the hashes above it and therefore changes the root.
example: A block header contains a Merkle root that students recompute from the block's transaction list.
scenario: A header must store one hash that commits to all transactions in the block. Which field is that?
scenarioWhy: The Merkle root is the one header hash that summarizes the block's transactions.

definition: A signed ledger operation that transfers value or calls a contract according to protocol rules.
wrongs: An unsigned note in a group chat about wanting to send coins.
A block header with no payment or contract call.
A seed phrase written for backup.
why: Nodes accept a transaction only if its signatures and rules check out, then a block may include it.
example: A signed payment names inputs and outputs, and a node relays it after the signature checks succeed.
scenario: A wallet produces a signed payment that nodes can check and miners may include. What object is that?
scenarioWhy: A transaction is the signed operation that moves value or invokes a contract.

definition: An output from an earlier transaction that has not yet been used as an input of a later one.
wrongs: An output that a later transaction has already consumed.
The Merkle root of a block.
A validator's locked staking deposit.
why: In the UTXO model, spendable coins are exactly the outputs that no later input has consumed.
example: A Bitcoin wallet lists an output from last week's payment because no later transaction has spent it.
scenario: A Bitcoin wallet shows coins that can still be spent because no later input has consumed them. What are those coins?
scenarioWrongs: Staking deposits on a proof-of-stake chain
scenarioWhy: An unspent transaction output is an output that has not been used as a later input.

definition: Competing to produce a valid proof-of-work block and thereby append it to the chain.
wrongs: Locking coins to be selected as a proof-of-stake validator.
Writing down a seed phrase on paper.
Browsing a block explorer without producing blocks.
why: Miners perform the proof-of-work search and, if successful, publish a block other nodes can check.
example: A teaching miner changes the nonce repeatedly until a test-network header hash meets the easy target.
scenario: Participants search for a header hash that meets a work target so they can publish the next block. What is that activity?
scenarioWhy: Mining is the competition to find a valid proof-of-work block.

definition: A measure of how hard it is to find a block hash that the proof-of-work rules will accept.
wrongs: The number of words in a seed phrase.
The size of a wallet's address book.
The color theme of a block explorer.
why: The protocol adjusts difficulty so that blocks arrive near the intended average interval.
example: Bitcoin raises difficulty when blocks have been found faster than the ten-minute target pace.
scenario: Blocks are being found much faster than the protocol intends. Which proof-of-work setting should rise?
scenarioWhy: Difficulty controls how hard it is to find an acceptable proof-of-work hash.

definition: New coins, often plus fees, that the protocol pays to the producer of a valid block.
wrongs: A fine taken from a validator for breaking consensus rules.
A seed phrase given to the block producer.
The parent hash stored in the header.
why: The reward compensates the producer and, on many public chains, is how new coins enter circulation.
example: A Bitcoin block's first transaction pays the miner the current subsidy plus the fees of included transactions.
scenario: A protocol mints new coins for the node that publishes a valid block. What is that payment called?
scenarioWhy: The block reward is the protocol payment to the producer of a valid block.

definition: An amount offered to the block producer for including a transaction in a block.
wrongs: The new-coin subsidy paid even when a block contains no user transactions.
The price of a hardware wallet in a store.
A tax printed on a paper receipt outside the protocol.
why: Producers have limited block space, so the offered fee influences which valid transactions they include.
example: A wallet adds a small fee so a test-network miner will include the student's transaction in the next block.
scenario: Block space is limited, and a user wants a producer to include one valid payment. What do they attach to the payment?
scenarioWhy: A transaction fee is the amount offered for inclusion in a block.

definition: A node's temporary set of valid transactions that are waiting to be included in a block.
wrongs: The permanent set of blocks already buried under thousands of confirmations.
A cold wallet stored in a safe.
The genesis block of the chain.
why: Transactions reach nodes before a block includes them, and the mempool holds those pending transactions.
example: After a student broadcasts a payment, a node shows it in the mempool until a block includes it.
scenario: A valid payment has been broadcast but is not in a block yet. Where does a node typically hold it?
scenarioWhy: The mempool is the waiting area for valid transactions that are not yet in a block.

definition: Inclusion of a transaction in a block, with another confirmation added by each later block built on that chain.
wrongs: A phone notification that a wallet app finished installing.
A bank employee saying a wire looks familiar.
A miner announcing an intention before any block exists.
why: Each added block makes it harder for an alternative branch to remove that transaction.
example: A merchant waits until a payment sits six blocks deep before treating it as sufficiently confirmed.
scenario: A payment is in a block, and five more blocks have been built on that chain. How many confirmations does it have?
scenarioWhy: The including block is the first confirmation, and each of the five blocks on top adds another.

definition: A rule tightening under which blocks valid by the new rules remain valid under the old rules.
wrongs: A rule change that old nodes treat as invalid, forcing every node to upgrade or split.
A temporary fork caused only by two miners finding blocks at the same moment.
A wallet update that changes only the app's color.
why: Old nodes still accept the stricter blocks, so the chain can upgrade without an immediate permanent split.
example: A soft-fork upgrade rejects a class of transactions that older rules would have allowed, while old nodes still accept the new blocks.
scenario: New rules reject some previously allowed transactions, but nodes that have not upgraded still accept the new blocks. Which change is that?
scenarioWhy: A soft fork tightens rules while keeping the new blocks acceptable to old nodes.

definition: A rule change that makes some blocks valid under the new rules invalid under the old rules.
wrongs: A tighter rule set whose new blocks old nodes still accept.
A display change in a wallet that does not affect consensus.
A backup of keys onto paper.
why: Nodes that do not upgrade will reject the new blocks, so the network can split if both sets continue.
example: A chain changes block format, and nodes that keep the old software reject the new blocks as invalid.
scenario: Upgraded nodes accept a new block format that non-upgraded nodes reject. Which kind of change is that?
scenarioWrongs: A theme update in a wallet
scenarioWhy: A hard fork creates blocks that old rules consider invalid, so non-upgraded nodes will not follow them.

definition: A node that downloads blocks and checks transactions itself against the consensus rules.
wrongs: A wallet that trusts a random website to say what the balance is, without checking blocks.
A block explorer run as a picture with no verification.
A miner that publishes blocks but never checks rules.
why: A full node keeps its own verified copy rather than trusting another server's claim about the ledger.
example: A lab computer runs a full node that rejects a test block whose transaction signatures do not verify.
scenario: A computer should reject invalid blocks itself instead of trusting a website's balance. What should it run?
scenarioWrongs: A wallet that trusts an unverified website
A publisher that skips rule checks
scenarioWhy: A full node downloads and validates the chain against the consensus rules on its own.

definition: A public identifier, often derived from a public key, that others use to send funds to a recipient.
wrongs: The secret seed that regenerates every private key in a wallet.
The difficulty target of the network.
The private key itself.
why: An address is meant to be shared so payers know where to send coins, without revealing the private key.
example: A student posts a test-network address on the class forum so others can send practice coins.
scenario: A student wants classmates to send practice coins without receiving any secret key. What should the student post?
scenarioWhy: An address is a public receiving identifier and does not reveal the private key.

definition: An ordered list of words from which a wallet can regenerate its private keys.
wrongs: A public receiving address safe to post on a forum.
The hash of the latest block.
A transaction fee quoted in the wallet.
why: Deterministic wallets derive the same keys from the same seed, so the word list is a backup of those keys.
example: After a phone is replaced, a wallet app regenerates the same test keys from the student's written seed phrase.
scenario: A wallet app on a new phone must recreate the same keys after the old phone is lost. Which backup does that?
scenarioWhy: The seed phrase is the word list a deterministic wallet uses to regenerate its private keys.

definition: A wallet whose private keys are present on a machine that is connected to a network.
wrongs: A wallet whose keys are generated and kept entirely offline.
A dedicated signing device that never exposes keys to the computer.
A watch-only display that holds no private keys at all.
why: Network exposure makes the keys easier to use and also more exposed to malware on that machine.
example: A phone wallet used for small test payments keeps its keys on the internet-connected phone.
scenario: Keys for small daily payments sit on an internet-connected phone. What kind of wallet is that?
scenarioWrongs: A watch-only view with no keys
scenarioWhy: A hot wallet stores private keys on a networked device.

definition: A wallet whose private keys are created and stored offline, away from networked computers.
wrongs: A wallet whose keys stay on an internet-connected phone.
A public block explorer account.
A full node that stores no user keys but is online.
why: Keeping keys offline reduces the chance that networked malware can copy them.
example: A club generates a savings-wallet seed on an offline computer and stores the written seed in a locked drawer.
scenario: A club wants long-term savings keys that never sit on an internet-connected computer. Which wallet type fits?
scenarioWrongs: A hot wallet on a phone
An online full node with no separate key storage
scenarioWhy: A cold wallet keeps the private keys offline.

definition: A unit that meters how much computation and storage a transaction may use on a smart-contract platform.
wrongs: The proof-of-work difficulty target.
The number of confirmations a merchant waits for.
The count of words in a seed phrase.
why: Metering computation stops a transaction from running without limit and prices the work nodes must do.
example: An Ethereum-style transaction states a gas limit so a looping call cannot run forever on every node.
scenario: A smart-contract call must have a metered limit so it cannot run forever on every node. What unit sets that budget?
scenarioWhy: Gas meters the computation and storage the call is allowed to consume.

definition: A proof-of-stake participant chosen to propose or attest to blocks according to the protocol.
wrongs: A proof-of-work miner searching for a hash below a target.
A block explorer that only displays data.
A hardware wallet with no role in consensus.
why: Validators take turns proposing or voting on blocks, and their stake can be rewarded or penalized.
example: A staked node is selected to propose the next block and broadcasts that block to the network.
scenario: A proof-of-stake network must choose a participant to propose the next block. What is that participant called?
scenarioWhy: A validator is the proof-of-stake participant selected to propose or attest to blocks.

definition: Locking coins so a participant can act as a validator under a proof-of-stake protocol.
wrongs: Spending electricity to search for a proof-of-work hash.
Publishing a receiving address on a website.
Downloading block headers without locking coins.
why: The locked stake is the economic bond that lets the protocol reward or penalize the validator.
example: A participant locks coins in a stake contract and then becomes eligible to attest to new blocks.
scenario: A holder wants to become eligible to attest on a proof-of-stake network by locking coins. What action is that?
scenarioWhy: Staking locks coins so the holder can participate as a proof-of-stake validator.

definition: The proof-of-work fork-choice rule that follows the chain with the most accumulated work.
wrongs: A rule that always prefers the chain with the fewest blocks.
A rule that lets each wallet pick a private history.
A rule that chooses the chain whose latest block has the largest fee.
why: Nodes adopt the chain that represents the greatest accumulated proof of work and switch if another chain overtakes it.
example: When two Bitcoin branches compete, nodes follow the branch whose total proof of work becomes greater.
scenario: Two proof-of-work branches compete, and nodes must pick one. Which rule tells them to follow the branch with the most accumulated work?
scenarioWrongs: Prefer the branch with the fewest blocks
Let each wallet keep a private history
Choose the branch with one large fee
scenarioWhy: The longest-chain rule, in proof of work, selects the chain with the most accumulated work.

definition: The compact block fields, including the parent hash, Merkle root, time, and consensus data, without the full transaction bodies.
wrongs: The complete list of every transaction's input scripts.
A wallet's seed phrase.
The human-readable name of a token.
why: The header is what gets hashed for the block hash and what links the block to its parent and transactions.
example: A light client stores Bitcoin headers, each containing a parent hash and a Merkle root, without every transaction body.
scenario: A light client stores parent hashes and Merkle roots but not every transaction body. Which part of each block is it keeping?
scenarioWhy: The block header holds the parent hash, Merkle root, and related fields without the full transaction bodies.

definition: The special first transaction in a block that creates the block reward for the block producer.
wrongs: A user payment that spends an earlier output.
A trade on a company that happens to share this technical name.
A contract call that only moves an existing token.
why: This transaction has no previous output; it is how the protocol introduces the reward into the block.
example: The first transaction in a Bitcoin block pays the miner the subsidy and fees and spends no earlier output.
scenario: The first transaction in a new block pays the miner and does not spend an earlier output. What is that transaction?
scenarioWrongs: A token transfer between two wallets
scenarioWhy: The coinbase transaction is the block's first transaction and the one that creates the block reward.

definition: A spending condition that requires valid signatures from more than one key before funds can move.
wrongs: A condition that any single leaked key can satisfy alone when the policy requires several.
A hash of the block with no keys involved.
A public address with no signing requirement.
why: The locking condition checks that the required number of distinct authorized signatures is present.
example: A club wallet moves funds only when two of three officers each provide a signature.
scenario: A club wants funds to move only when two of three officers sign. Which spending condition is that?
scenarioWrongs: A block hash with no signatures
A public address and no signature check
scenarioWhy: Multisignature requires more than one authorized signature before the funds can be spent.

definition: A shared record of transactions that many nodes maintain and update under consensus rules.
wrongs: A private spreadsheet that only one accountant can edit.
A paper notebook locked in one office.
A single bank database with no copies at other nodes.
why: Each participating node keeps a copy and applies the same rules to accept updates.
example: Several lab computers each store the class blockchain and accept a new block only when its proof checks.
scenario: Several nodes each keep a copy of the same transaction history and update it by shared rules. What is that record?
scenarioWrongs: One bank database with no other copies
scenarioWhy: A distributed ledger is the shared transaction record maintained by many nodes.

definition: The resistance of confirmed history to silent edits, because changing a block changes its hash and later links.
wrongs: The freedom to rewrite an old block in place without changing any later hash.
The ability of one wallet to edit another person's confirmed payment quietly.
A guarantee that no competing branch can ever exist even for one block.
why: The hash chain makes an in-place edit evident, since later blocks would no longer link to the edited block.
example: Changing one confirmed transaction in a class chain breaks the stored hash of that block and every following parent link.
scenario: Someone edits a confirmed transaction inside an old block but leaves later headers untouched. What will other nodes notice?
scenarioAnswer: Later hashes no longer link to that block
scenarioWrongs: Nothing, because old blocks can be edited in place
Only a change in the wallet's color theme
scenarioWhy: Immutability here means the edit changes the block hash, so the later links no longer match.

definition: A network in which nodes exchange blocks and transactions directly, without one server owning the ledger.
wrongs: A design in which only one company server is allowed to store the official ledger.
A phone call between two wallet owners.
A cable that connects a hardware wallet to a laptop.
why: Each node can relay to other nodes, so the ledger is not stored solely by a central operator.
example: A new lab node downloads blocks from several classmate nodes rather than from one official server.
scenario: Nodes pass blocks to one another, and no single server is the owner of the ledger. What kind of network is that?
scenarioWrongs: A single company server that alone stores the ledger
A USB cable to a hardware wallet
scenarioWhy: A peer-to-peer network lets nodes exchange ledger data directly without a central owner.

definition: A switch from one branch to another when the fork-choice rule decides the other branch is preferred.
wrongs: A permanent edit that changes an old block but keeps the same block hash.
A wallet renaming an address in its contact list.
A user increasing a transaction fee before broadcast.
why: Nodes replace the previous tip when a competing branch becomes the preferred chain under the fork-choice rule.
example: Nodes that briefly followed block A switch to a competing branch after that branch accumulates more proof of work.
scenario: Nodes were on branch A, then branch B accumulates more work and they adopt B instead. What is that switch called?
scenarioWrongs: An in-place edit that keeps the old hash
scenarioWhy: A chain reorganization is the adoption of a different branch under the fork-choice rule.

definition: The sibling hashes needed to recompute a Merkle root from one transaction and show that it was included.
wrongs: The private key of the transaction's sender.
A full copy of every transaction in every block.
The seed phrase of the block producer.
why: Given the transaction, the sibling hashes, and the root, a light client can check inclusion without the whole block body.
example: A light client receives a payment's sibling hashes and checks that they lead to the Merkle root in a header it already stores.
scenario: A light client knows a header's Merkle root and wants to check one payment was in that block without downloading every transaction. What does it need?
scenarioWhy: A Merkle proof supplies the sibling hashes that connect one transaction to the known root.

definition: A blockchain design that allows anyone who follows the protocol to run a node or attempt to produce blocks.
wrongs: A ledger where only a pre-approved organization list may validate transactions.
A private database with a single administrator account.
A wallet that requires a store receipt before it can display a balance.
why: Open participation is part of the design: identity approval is not required to join the network.
example: Anyone may start a Bitcoin full node and relay transactions without asking a central registrar for approval.
scenario: Anyone who follows the rules may run a node and try to produce blocks, with no membership approval. Which design is that?
scenarioWrongs: A ledger limited to a pre-approved validator list
A wallet that requires a store receipt
scenarioWhy: A permissionless blockchain lets anyone participate by following the protocol.

definition: A blockchain design in which a known set of organizations controls who may validate or write transactions.
wrongs: A network that lets any stranger produce blocks without approval.
A public proof-of-work chain with anonymous miners.
A paper ledger with no computers.
why: Membership is restricted, so the validators' identities are known to the governing organizations.
example: A consortium of universities runs a ledger where only the member registrars' nodes may validate new blocks.
scenario: Only approved university registrars may validate blocks on a shared ledger. Which design is that?
scenarioWrongs: An open network any stranger may mine
A public chain with anonymous miners
scenarioWhy: A permissioned blockchain limits validation to a known, approved set of participants.

definition: The family of protocols that combine hash-linked blocks with a probabilistic fork-choice rule such as proof of work.
wrongs: A vote among a fixed committee that finalizes each block with no chain of hashes.
A single administrator who overwrites a database row.
A wallet standard for deriving addresses.
why: Nakamoto consensus uses the chain structure and accumulated work so nodes can agree without a fixed voting committee.
example: Bitcoin nodes follow Nakamoto consensus when they adopt the proof-of-work chain with the most accumulated work.
scenario: Nodes agree by extending hash-linked blocks and preferring the chain with the most proof of work, with no fixed committee. Which consensus family is that?
scenarioWrongs: A fixed committee vote with no hash chain
scenarioWhy: Nakamoto consensus is the hash-chain, probabilistic fork-choice design introduced with Bitcoin.

definition: A protocol penalty that takes part of a validator's stake for provably breaking consensus rules.
wrongs: A bonus paid for producing a valid block.
A refund of unused gas to a contract caller.
A wallet feature that hides small balances.
why: The penalty makes specified misbehavior, such as signing two conflicting blocks, costly for the validator.
example: A proof-of-stake protocol destroys part of a validator's locked coins after evidence shows the validator signed two conflicting blocks.
scenario: A validator signs two conflicting blocks for the same duty, and the protocol can prove it. What can happen to the locked stake?
scenarioAnswer: Part of the stake can be slashed
scenarioWrongs: The validator must receive a larger block reward
The stake is converted into a public seed phrase
scenarioWhy: Slashing is the protocol's penalty that removes part of the stake for provable rule breaking.

definition: A dedicated device that holds private keys and signs transactions without exposing those keys to the attached computer.
wrongs: A phone app that stores private keys in ordinary application memory on a networked phone.
A website that displays block hashes.
A full node that stores the ledger but not the user's keys.
why: The keys stay on the device, and the computer receives a signature rather than the key itself.
example: A treasurer connects a hardware wallet, confirms the payment on the device screen, and the computer receives only the signature.
scenario: A computer may prepare a payment, but the private key should stay inside a separate signing device. Which device is that?
scenarioWrongs: A networked phone app that stores the key in ordinary memory
A full node with no user keys
scenarioWhy: A hardware wallet signs inside the device so the attached computer does not receive the private key.

definition: The requirement that honest nodes, given the same state and transaction, compute the same result.
wrongs: The idea that each node may freely compute a different contract result and still agree.
The requirement that a wallet show a different balance on every screen refresh.
The rule that miners ignore transaction contents.
why: Consensus about contract state is possible only if every honest node reaches the same result.
example: Two Ethereum-style nodes process the same vote transaction and both store the same new vote total.
scenario: Two honest nodes process the same contract call from the same state. What must their results be?
scenarioWrongs: Different results that are both final
A result chosen by each wallet's theme
No result, because contract code is ignored
scenarioWhy: Deterministic execution means the same inputs produce the same contract result on every honest node.

definition: The number of proof-of-work hash attempts a miner or a whole network can perform per second.
wrongs: The number of seed words stored in a wallet backup.
The number of addresses in a contact list.
The number of smart contracts a wallet can display.
why: A higher hash rate means more attempts per second to find a header hash that meets the target.
example: A teaching dashboard reports that the lab's test miner is trying one thousand header hashes each second.
scenario: A dashboard counts how many proof-of-work header hashes the lab miner tries each second. What quantity is that?
scenarioWhy: Hash rate measures proof-of-work hash attempts per second.

definition: The condition under which a protocol treats a block as irreversible, either after deep confirmation or explicit finalization.
wrongs: The moment a transaction is typed but not yet broadcast.
The display of an unconfirmed payment sitting only in a mempool.
A wallet's local note that the user hopes a payment will succeed.
why: Finality describes when the protocol's rules say a block should no longer be replaced by a competing branch.
example: After a proof-of-stake checkpoint is finalized, nodes treat that block as irreversible under the protocol's assumptions.
scenario: A protocol checkpoint is finalized, and nodes will no longer replace that block under their rules. What condition has the block reached?
scenarioWrongs: It is still only typed on a screen
It sits unconfirmed in the mempool
It is only a user's private hope
scenarioWhy: Finality is the protocol condition that treats the block as irreversible.
